quiz.stem:
A 71-year-old woman has a DXA scan showing a lumbar spine T-score of -2.8 and a femoral neck T-score of -2.6. She has never had a fracture. Her calcium and vitamin D levels are normal, and she has no oesophageal disease. She is prescribed weekly oral alendronate.

Which instruction is most important for her to follow?
options: Take it with food to prevent stomach upset
Take it at bedtime with milk
Take it fasting with a full glass of plain water and remain upright for 30 minutes before eating
Take it with a calcium supplement to improve absorption
quiz.explanation: Oral bisphosphonates are **very poorly absorbed**, and absorption is almost abolished by food, calcium and other drinks. They also cause **oesophageal irritation and ulceration** if they lodge in the oesophagus. So they are taken **on an empty stomach first thing in the morning with a full glass of plain water**, the patient must **stay upright for at least 30 minutes**, and then wait before food, other drinks, calcium or other medicines. Her T-score of -2.5 or lower confirms osteoporosis.
whyWrong: Food markedly reduces absorption.
Lying down after the dose risks oesophagitis, and milk reduces absorption.
Calcium binds the drug and prevents absorption; take separately.
Chewing increases oesophageal and oral irritation.

quiz.stem:
A 74-year-old woman has been on denosumab injections every 6 months for 4 years. She tells her GP that she feels well, has read about jaw problems online and wants to stop. Her last injection was 5 months ago.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop denosumab now; no further treatment is needed
Delay the next injection by 12 months as a drug holiday
Switch to calcium and vitamin D alone
Explain the rebound fracture risk; if stopping, transition to a bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid) timed to the next due dose
Double the dose to shorten the course
quiz.explanation: Denosumab's effect **wears off rapidly** after the dosing interval, causing **rebound increased bone turnover**, rapid bone loss and a risk of **multiple vertebral fractures**. It must **not be stopped or delayed without follow-on therapy**, usually a **bisphosphonate** such as zoledronic acid given around when the next dose is due. Drug holidays apply to bisphosphonates, not denosumab. Discuss her concerns: osteonecrosis of the jaw is very rare at osteoporosis doses, and good dental hygiene and regular dental review reduce the risk.
whyWrong: Stopping without follow-on therapy risks rebound vertebral fractures.
Drug holidays are not safe with denosumab.
Calcium and vitamin D alone will not prevent rebound bone loss.
There is no role for dose doubling.
quiz.ausPearl: Denosumab rebound fractures after cessation are a recognised Australian prescribing safety issue highlighted in PBS and RACGP guidance.

quiz.stem:
A 42-year-old man presents with acute back pain after lifting a light box. X-ray shows a wedge fracture of L1. DXA shows a lumbar spine Z-score of -3.1. He drinks little alcohol and does not smoke. He has had intermittent diarrhoea and bloating for years.

Which investigation is most likely to reveal the cause?
options: Coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA)
quiz.explanation: A **minimal-trauma vertebral fracture** in a **young man** with a very low **Z-score** strongly suggests **secondary osteoporosis**, and the history of chronic diarrhoea and bloating points to **coeliac disease**, which causes malabsorption of calcium and vitamin D. Investigate with **tTG-IgA and total IgA**, along with calcium, vitamin D, PTH, testosterone, thyroid and renal function, and serum protein electrophoresis. Treating the cause (gluten-free diet) improves bone density. Other causes in young men include hypogonadism, glucocorticoid use, hyperthyroidism and myeloma.
whyWrong: PSA is not relevant to his age and presentation.
HLA-B27 relates to spondyloarthritis, not osteoporotic fracture.
Uric acid relates to gout.
A bone scan does not identify the cause of low bone density.

lessons.title: Paediatric orthopaedics and the limping child
objectives: Build an age-based differential for the limping child
Distinguish transient synovitis from septic arthritis using clinical and laboratory features
Recognise Perthes disease, SUFE and developmental dysplasia of the hip
Manage common paediatric fractures and identify patterns suggesting non-accidental injury

sections.heading: The limping child
sections.body:
Limp is a common paediatric presentation. Most causes are benign (minor trauma, transient synovitis), but the AMC wants you to exclude **septic arthritis**, **SUFE**, **non-accidental injury** and, rarely, **malignancy** (leukaemia, bone tumours). Age is the best starting point:

| Age | Think of |
|---|---|
| 0-3 years | Septic arthritis, **DDH**, **toddler's fracture**, **NAI** |
| 3-10 years | **Transient synovitis**, septic arthritis, **Perthes disease**, fracture |
| 10-16 years | **SUFE**, Osgood-Schlatter, sports injuries, bone tumours |

Any age: infection (septic arthritis, osteomyelitis), trauma, leukaemia, juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

Guidance from the **RCH Melbourne clinical practice guidelines** is widely used in Australia.

sections.heading: Mechanisms worth knowing
sections.body:
- **Transient synovitis:** a self-limiting, post-viral inflammation of the hip synovium.
- **Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis:** haematogenous spread to the metaphysis (rich, slow-flowing blood supply); in young children, metaphyseal vessels cross the growth plate into the joint. **S. aureus** is commonest; **Kingella kingae** is important under 4 years.
- **Perthes disease:** idiopathic **avascular necrosis of the femoral head** in children aged about 4-8 (boys more than girls); the head collapses and remodels over 2-4 years.
- **SUFE (slipped upper femoral epiphysis):** the femoral head slips posteriorly and inferiorly through the weakened growth plate during the adolescent growth spurt; risk factors are **obesity**, male sex and endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, growth hormone therapy).
- **DDH:** abnormal development of the hip, from mild dysplasia to dislocation; risk factors are **breech presentation, family history, female sex, first-born** and tight swaddling with legs straight.

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.body:
**Transient synovitis:** age 3-8, recent viral URTI, **well-looking**, afebrile or low-grade fever, limp or reluctance to walk, mildly reduced hip movement.

**Septic arthritis:** unwell, febrile, **refuses to weight bear**, holds the hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, severe pain on any movement.

**Kocher criteria** (predict septic arthritis of the hip): **non-weight bearing, fever over 38.5°C, ESR over 40 mm/h, WCC over 12 x 10^9/L**. The more present, the higher the probability (CRP over 20 mg/L is often added).

**Perthes:** insidious limp, hip, thigh or **knee pain**, reduced abduction and internal rotation.

**SUFE:** overweight adolescent, hip, thigh or **knee pain** (referred along the obturator nerve), limp, **loss of internal rotation**, and **obligatory external rotation when the hip is flexed**. It can be bilateral.

**DDH:** asymmetric skin creases, leg length difference, limited abduction; in newborns, **Barlow** (dislocatable) and **Ortolani** (relocates with a clunk) tests; in older children, a painless limp or waddling gait.

**Other common problems:**
- **Toddler's fracture:** spiral undisplaced tibial fracture in a newly walking child, refuses to weight bear, may be invisible on initial X-ray
- **Osgood-Schlatter disease:** active adolescent, pain and a tender lump at the **tibial tuberosity**, worse with running and kneeling; self-limiting
- **Bone tumours:** night pain, persistent pain, swelling; **osteosarcoma** at the metaphysis around the knee in adolescents; **Ewing sarcoma** in the diaphysis, often with fever

sections.heading: Investigations
sections.body:
- **Bloods:** FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures if febrile; blood film if leukaemia suspected
- **Hip ultrasound** shows an effusion (present in both transient synovitis and septic arthritis) and guides aspiration
- **Joint aspiration** if septic arthritis is suspected
- **X-ray:** AP pelvis and **frog-leg lateral** views for Perthes and **SUFE** (frog-leg lateral shows a subtle slip that an AP can miss; on AP, **Klein's line** along the superior femoral neck fails to intersect the epiphysis)
- **DDH:** **hip ultrasound** in infants under about 4-6 months (femoral head is cartilage); X-ray after that. Infants with risk factors (breech, family history) have an ultrasound at around 6 weeks per local guidance
- **MRI:** early Perthes, osteomyelitis, tumours
- Suspected NAI: skeletal survey per local child protection protocol

sections.heading: Management
sections.body:
**Transient synovitis:** rest and NSAIDs (ibuprofen); improves within days. Review within 24-48 hours, with advice to return if fever develops or the child won't walk. Symptoms beyond about a week need reassessment.

**Septic arthritis:** urgent orthopaedic referral for **aspiration and washout**, **IV antibiotics** per local guideline (e.g. flucloxacillin or cefazolin, per RCH or eTG), then oral step-down.

**Perthes:** orthopaedic referral; maintain range of movement, physiotherapy, activity modification, bracing or surgery in some; younger age at onset has a better prognosis.

**SUFE:** an **orthopaedic emergency**. Make the child **non-weight bearing** immediately (crutches or wheelchair) and arrange urgent **surgical pinning** in situ, as further slip risks avascular necrosis.

**DDH:** **Pavlik harness** in early infancy; closed or open reduction and casting later. Late diagnosis worsens outcomes.

**Paediatric fractures:**
- **Buckle (torus) fracture** of the distal radius: stable, removable splint for about 3 weeks, **no routine follow-up**
- **Greenstick fractures:** may need reduction if angulated
- **Supracondylar humerus fracture** (age about 5-7, FOOSH): check **radial pulse, hand perfusion** and nerves (anterior interosseous nerve: test the "OK" sign); displaced fractures need urgent reduction and pinning; a pulseless, poorly perfused hand is an emergency; watch for compartment syndrome (Volkmann's)
- **Pulled elbow** (radial head subluxation, age 1-4): child pulled by the arm, holds arm pronated and won't use it; **reduce by supination-flexion or hyperpronation** without X-ray if the history is typical

**Non-accidental injury clues:** fractures in non-ambulant infants, **posterior rib fractures**, **metaphyseal corner fractures**, multiple fractures of different ages, a mechanism that doesn't match development, delay in presentation. Involve the child protection unit and report as required by state law.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Febrile child who won't weight bear with high ESR and WCC: **septic arthritis**, aspirate and wash out. Well child after a cold: transient synovitis.
- Overweight 13-year-old with **knee pain** and limp: examine the **hip**; SUFE until proven otherwise; **frog-leg lateral** X-ray and **non-weight bearing**.
- A buckle fracture needs a splint, not a cast and fracture clinic.
- A pulled elbow in a toddler: reduce without imaging.
- A fracture in an infant who can't walk: think NAI.

keyPoints: Limp by age: 0-3 DDH, toddler's fracture, NAI; 3-10 transient synovitis, Perthes; 10-16 SUFE.
Kocher criteria for septic arthritis: non-weight bearing, fever over 38.5°C, ESR over 40, WCC over 12.
Septic arthritis: aspiration, washout and IV antibiotics; S. aureus, and Kingella under 4.
SUFE: obese adolescent with knee pain, loss of internal rotation; frog-leg lateral X-ray; non-weight bearing and urgent pinning.
Perthes: avascular necrosis of the femoral head, boys aged 4-8.
DDH: Barlow and Ortolani in newborns; ultrasound under about 4-6 months; Pavlik harness.
Buckle fractures need a removable splint and no follow-up; pulled elbow is reduced without X-ray.
redFlags: Fever with refusal to weight bear
Adolescent with knee or hip pain and loss of internal rotation (SUFE)
Night pain, weight loss or pallor and bruising (tumour or leukaemia)
Fracture in a non-ambulant child or mechanism inconsistent with development

contrast.india: Often placed in a plaster cast with fracture clinic follow-up.
contrast.australia: Removable splint for about 3 weeks without routine follow-up (RCH guidance).

contrast.india: Clinical examination at birth; ultrasound less often.
contrast.australia: Clinical checks at birth and 6-8 weeks with hip ultrasound for infants with risk factors.

quiz.stem:
A 5-year-old boy has had a limp for 2 days. He had a cold last week. He is playing happily in the waiting room. Temperature is 37.4°C. He walks with a limp but will bear weight, and there is mild restriction of right hip internal rotation. WCC is 9.2 x 10^9/L, ESR 12 mm/h, CRP 6 mg/L.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.explanation: A **well child aged 3-8** with a limp after a **viral illness**, **weight bearing**, **afebrile** and with **normal inflammatory markers** has **transient synovitis**. He meets **none of the Kocher criteria** (non-weight bearing, fever over 38.5°C, ESR over 40, WCC over 12), so septic arthritis is very unlikely. Treat with NSAIDs and rest and review within 24-48 hours, with advice to return if fever or refusal to walk develops. Perthes has an insidious course; SUFE affects adolescents; JIA needs symptoms for at least 6 weeks.
whyWrong: He meets none of the Kocher criteria and looks well.
Perthes presents with an insidious limp over weeks, not after a cold.
SUFE affects adolescents, typically overweight.
JIA requires arthritis persisting for at least 6 weeks.

quiz.stem:
A 13-year-old boy with a BMI above the 95th centile presents with 3 weeks of left knee pain and a limp. Examination of the knee is normal. When his left hip is flexed, it rotates externally, and internal rotation is markedly reduced.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Blood tests for inflammatory markers only
AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral X-rays of both hips, and make him non-weight bearing
quiz.explanation: An **overweight adolescent** with **knee pain** (referred from the hip via the obturator nerve), a **normal knee examination**, **loss of internal rotation** and **obligatory external rotation on hip flexion** has a **slipped upper femoral epiphysis** until proven otherwise. Obtain **AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral** X-rays of **both hips** (it is bilateral in a significant minority). Make him **non-weight bearing** immediately and refer urgently for **pinning in situ**, because further slip increases the risk of avascular necrosis. **Rule:** knee pain in a child means examine the hip.
whyWrong: The knee is normal; the pain is referred from the hip.
Physiotherapy would miss a SUFE, and ongoing weight bearing risks further slip.
Delay risks progression of the slip and avascular necrosis.
Blood tests do not diagnose SUFE.

quiz.stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because she won't use her left arm. Her father says he pulled her up by the hand when she was about to run onto the road. She is holding the arm by her side, slightly flexed and pronated. There is no swelling or bruising, and she is otherwise happy.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reduce by supination and flexion, or hyperpronation, without an X-ray
X-ray the elbow before any manipulation
Refer to the child protection unit
Arrange an ultrasound of the elbow
quiz.explanation: This is a classic **pulled elbow** (radial head subluxation): a child aged about 1-4, a **pulling mechanism** on an extended arm, and a child who holds the arm **pronated** and won't use it, with no swelling or bruising. The annular ligament slips over the radial head. Management is **reduction without imaging** when the history is typical: **supination and flexion** or **hyperpronation**; a click may be felt, and the child usually uses the arm within minutes. X-ray is needed only if the history is atypical, there is swelling or bruising, or reduction fails. Explain the mechanism to the parents to prevent recurrence. The mechanism here is accidental and consistent.
whyWrong: Imaging is unnecessary with a typical history and no swelling.
Casting is not needed once reduced.
The mechanism is consistent and accidental; no child protection concern is evident.
Ultrasound is not required for a typical pulled elbow.
